transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Dr Farrant. You're Keturah?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I can hear you're a bit wheezy. Take your time. What's been happening?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I've had a cold for a few days, and since yesterday my asthma's gone really bad.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: How often have you been using your blue inhaler?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About twice a day.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Is that right?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Honestly, no. Since last night it's been every two hours, maybe more.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Thank you for being honest, that's important. Does it help?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: For about an hour, then it comes back.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Are you on a brown or purple preventer inhaler as well?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: The brown one, Clenil. I'm meant to take it twice a day, but I forget a lot.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: What dose is it?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: 100. Two puffs.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Have you ever been in hospital with your asthma?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Once, about three years ago. I was in for two nights.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Did you ever need intensive care, or a breathing tube?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, never.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any chest pain, or coughing up anything?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just a tight chest. A bit of clear phlegm.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any fevers?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I was a bit hot a couple of days ago, with the cold.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Do you smoke?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No, but I vape every day.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any other medicines?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Any allergies?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Aspirin. It makes my chest go tight. I had to go to hospital once after taking it.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's really important, thank you. So no aspirin or anti-inflammatories like ibuprofen for you. Let me examine you. You're speaking in full sentences, which is good. Your breathing rate is 24, heart rate 108, oxygen levels 95 percent on air. I can hear wheeze all over your chest, on both sides, but air is getting in everywhere. Can you blow into this peak flow meter for me?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: (blows)

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: That's 250. What's your best?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: About 450.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: So that's about 55 percent of your best. This is a moderate asthma attack. We'll give you a nebuliser now with salbutamol, five milligrams, and I'm going to start you on steroid tablets, prednisolone, 40 milligrams once a day for five days.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Let's see how you are after the nebuliser.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: (later) That's much better.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: Your peak flow is now 380, about 84 percent of your best, and your breathing rate is 18. Oxygen 98 percent. That's a good response.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Can I go home?

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If you stay this well for the next hour, yes. Before you go, the nurse will check how you use your inhalers. It's really important to use the brown one every day, even when you feel well.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I know. I'll try.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: I want you to see your GP or asthma nurse within two working days, to review your inhalers and make an asthma action plan.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Clinician
transcript.text: If you need your blue inhaler more than every four hours, if you're too breathless to speak, or your lips go blue, call 999 straight away.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Okay, thank you.

reference_note.presenting_complaint: Worsening wheeze and breathlessness since yesterday, with a viral upper respiratory infection.
reference_note.history: Initially reported using salbutamol twice a day; on questioning, using salbutamol every 2 hours since last night, with only brief relief. Prescribed Clenil 100 micrograms two puffs twice daily but adherence poor. Tight chest, small amount of clear sputum; feverish two days ago. One previous hospital admission 3 years ago (two nights); never required intensive care. Uses an e-cigarette daily.
reference_note.medications_allergies: Salbutamol inhaler as required. Clenil (beclometasone) 100 micrograms, two puffs twice daily. Aspirin allergy (bronchospasm, previously needed hospital treatment); avoid NSAIDs.
reference_note.examination: Speaking in full sentences. RR 24, HR 108, SpO2 95% on air. Widespread bilateral wheeze with good air entry. PEF 250 L/min (best 450, about 55%). After salbutamol 5 mg nebulised: PEF 380 (about 84%), RR 18, SpO2 98%.
reference_note.impression: Moderate acute asthma exacerbation triggered by a viral infection; good response to bronchodilator. Poor preventer adherence.
reference_note.plan: Prednisolone 40 mg once daily for 5 days. Inhaler technique check before discharge. Discharge if stable after one hour of observation. GP or asthma nurse review within 2 working days for inhaler review and asthma action plan.
reference_note.safety_netting: Call 999 if salbutamol needed more often than every 4 hours, too breathless to speak, or blue lips.

mutations.seeded_rationale: Two-hourly reliever use marks a severe exacerbation; the original figure understates severity and could lead to premature discharge or inadequate follow-up.

mutations.seeded_rationale: Aspirin-sensitive asthma means NSAIDs can trigger a severe attack; without the allergy recorded she may be given ibuprofen.

mutations.seeded_rationale: Salbutamol (short-acting reliever) recorded as salmeterol (long-acting bronchodilator), a recognised sound-alike pair; salmeterol is slow to act and must not be used as a reliever or without an inhaled steroid, so a prescription copied from this note could leave her without a reliever during an attack.
Inability to complete sentences is a feature of acute severe asthma; the record overstates severity and contradicts the decision to discharge.
